# Research Plan: NASA Space Shuttle Construction Milestones & EAFB Landings

## Goal
Identify the Space Shuttle with the second fewest construction milestones before 2024, then list its missions that landed at Edwards Air Force Base (EAFB).

## Components
1. **NASA Space Shuttle Reference Guide** — Locate the authoritative NASA reference guide detailing all Space Shuttles with construction milestones
2. **Construction Milestones per Shuttle** — Extract construction milestone counts for each orbiter (Enterprise, Columbia, Challenger, Discovery, Atlantis, Endeavour) before 2024
3. **Rank Shuttles by Milestone Count** — Determine which shuttle has the second fewest milestones
4. **Flight History of Target Shuttle** — Get complete flight manifest for that shuttle
5. **EAFB Landing Missions** — Filter flights to those landing at Edwards Air Force Base

## Constraints
- Use only NASA or authoritative government sources
- Construction milestones must be dated before 2024
- Output: ranked list of shuttles by milestone count, then EAFB missions for the 2nd fewest

## Queries
1. **High** — "NASA Space Shuttle reference guide construction milestones all orbiters official documentation"
2. **High** — "NASA orbiter construction milestones timeline Enterprise Columbia Challenger Discovery Atlantis Endeavour"
3. **Medium** — "Space Shuttle flight landing sites Edwards Air Force Base EAFB missions by orbiter"
4. **Medium** — "NASA Space Shuttle program orbiter construction history milestones completed before 2024"
5. **Low** — "Space Shuttle orbiter delivery dates construction completion milestones NASA facts"

{"content": "800|Cook’s achievements on Endeavour were numerous, including the accurate charting of New Zealand and Australia and successfully navigating the Great Barrier Reef. Thousands of new plant specimens and animal species were observed and illustrated on this maiden voyage. Cook also established the usefulness of including scientists on voyages of exploration.
801|
802|Space Shuttle Endeavour embodies similar experiences. Its first launch, the STS-49 mission, began with a flawless liftoff on May 7, 1992, beginning a journey filled with excitement, anticipation and many firsts.
803|
804|One of Endeavour’s primary assignments was to capture INTELSAT VI, an orbiting, but not functioning, communications satellite, and replace its rocket motor. Unfortunately, the Space Shuttle wasn’t designed to retrieve the satellite, which created many repair challenges.
805|
806|The project sparked public interest in the mission and NASA received a deluge of suggestions on possible ways for the crew to grab onto the satellite. It took three attempts to capture the satellite for repairs to be made. An unprecedented three-person spacewalk took place after the procedure was evaluated by the astronauts and ground team.
807|
808|Between rescue attempts, the STS-49 crew was busy with a variety of activities. They conducted medical tests assessing the human body’s performance in microgravity, and recorded footage for an educational video comparing Cook’s first voyage on Endeavour with the Space Shuttle orbiter’s maiden voyage.
809|
810|Once the new motor was attached, it propelled the satellite into the correct orbit, providing a relay link for the equivalent of 120,000 two-way simultaneous telephone calls and three television channels.
811|
812|This was the first time four spacewalks were conducted on a Space Shuttle mission and one of them was the longest in space history, lasting more than eight hours.
813|
814|The crew also took part in the Commercial Protein Crystal Growth experiment. The research tested the production of protein crystals grown in microgravity.
815|
816|Because of Endeavour’s excellent performance, NASA decided to extend the flight two days to complete more mission objectives and allow the crew enough time to prepare for landing.
817|
818|OV-105 became the first Space Shuttle orbiter to use a drag chute during a landing — only one of many technical improvements made to Endeavour.
819|
820|Just as James Cook set the standard with his seafaring Endeavour voyage, the Space Shuttle Endeavour missions have continued to uphold and surpass the standards set by its namesake, more than 200 years later.
821|
822|**Construction Milestones**
823|
824|February 15, 1982: Start structural assembly of Crew Module  
825|July 31, 1987: Contract Award  
826|September 28, 1987: Start structural assembly of aft-fuselage  
827|December 22, 1987: Wings arrive at Palmdale, Calif. from Grumman  
828|August 1, 1987: Start of Final Assembly  
829|July 6, 1990: Completed final assembly  
830|April 25, 1991: Rollout from Palmdale  
831|May 7, 1991: Delivery to Kennedy Space Center  
832|April 6, 1992: Flight Readiness Firing  
833|May 7, 1992: First Flight (STS-49)
834|
835|**Upgrades and Features**
836|
837|Spare parts from the construction of Discovery (OV-103) and Atlantis (OV-104), manufactured to facilitate the repair of an orbiter if needed, were eventually used to build OV-105.
838|
839|Endeavour also featured new hardware, designed to improve and expand orbiter capabilities. Most of this equipment was later incorporated into the other three orbiters during out-of-service major inspection and modification programs.
840|
841|Endeavour’s upgrades include:
842|
843|* A 40-foot-diameter drag chute that reduces the orbiter’s rollout distance by 1,000 to 2,000 feet.
844|* An updated avionics system that include advanced general purpose computers, improved inertial measurement units and tactical air navigation systems, enhanced master events controllers and multiplexer-demultiplexers, a solid-state star tracker.
845|* Improved nose wheel steering mechanisms.
846|* An improved version of the Auxiliary Power Units that provide power to operate the Space Shuttle’s hydraulic systems.
847|* Installation of an external airlock, making Endeavour capable of docking with the International Space Station.
848|* Originally equipped as the first extended duration orbiter, later removed during OMDP to save weight for ISS missions.
849|* Installation of a ground cooling hookup to allow payload bay to cool the mini-pressurized logistics module (MPLM).
850|* General weight-reduction program to maximize the payload capability to the ISS.
851|* Doublers added to several wing spars to allow heavier payloads and two wing glove truss tubes were replaced with units having increased wall thickness.
852|* Approximately 100 modifications made to Endeavour during its first Orbiter Major Modification period (OMDP).
853|
854|Space Shuttle Endeavour’s OMDP began in December 2003. Engineers and technicians spent 900,000 hours performing 124 modifications to the vehicle. These included recommended return to flight safety modifications, bonding more than 1,000 thermal protection system tiles and inspecting more than 150 miles of wiring. Eighty five of the modifications are complete and 39 are still underway.
855|
856|Two of the more extensive modifications included the addition of the multi-functional electronic display system (glass cockpit), and the three-string global positioning system.
857|
858|The glass cockpit is a new, full-color, flat-panel display system that improves interaction between the crew and orbiter. It provides easy-to-read graphics portraying key flight indicators like attitude display and mach speed. Endeavour was the last vehicle in the fleet to receive this system.
859|
860|The three-string global positioning system will improve the shuttle’s landing capability. It will allow Endeavour to make a landing at any runway long enough to handle the shuttle. The previous system only allowed for landings at military bases. Shuttle major modification periods are scheduled at regular intervals to enhance safety and performance, infuse new technology and allow thorough inspections of the airframe and wiring. This was the second of modification period performed entirely at Kennedy. Endeavour’s previous modification was completed in March 1997.
861|
862|Endeavour has undergone extensive modifications, including the addition of all of the return-to-flight safety upgrades added to both Discovery and Atlantis.
863|
864|Endeavour’s flight on mission STS-118 was the first launch for the orbiter in more than four years.
865|
866|**[Flights of Endeavour](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/2011.05.09-endeavour.pdf?emrc=e95086)**
867|
868|## Orbiter Atlantis (OV-104)
869|
870|ISS028-E-015831 (10 July 2011) — The space shuttle Atlantis is pictured prior to a perfect docking with the International Space Station at 10:07 a.m. (CDT). Part of a Russian Progress spacecraft which is docked to the station is in the foreground.
871|
872|**Atlantis’s Final Launch**
873|
874|Space shuttle Commander Chris Ferguson and crewmates Pilot Doug Hurley, and Mission Specialists Sandy Magnus and Rex Walheim are on their way to the International Space Station after launching from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center at 11:29 a.m. EDT on Friday, July 8. STS-135 is the final mission of NASA’s Space Shuttle Program. The 12-day mission will deliver the Raffaello multi-purpose logistics module filled with more than 8,000 pounds of supplies and spare parts to sustain space station operations after the shuttles are retired. STS-135 is the 135th shuttle flight, the 33rd flight for Atlantis and the 37th shuttle mission dedicated to station assembly and maintenance.
875|
876|NASA’s fourth space-rated space shuttle, OV-104 “Atlantis,” was named after the two-masted boat that served as the primary research vessel for the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute in Massachusetts from 1930 to 1966. The boat had a 17-member crew and accommodated up to five scientists who worked in two onboard laboratories, examining water samples and marine life. The crew also used the first electronic sounding devices to map the ocean floor.
877|
878|Construction of the orbiter Atlantis began on March 3, 1980. Thanks to lessons learned in the construction and testing of orbiters Enterprise, Columbia and Challenger, Atlantis was completed in about half the time in man-hours spent on Columbia. This is largely attributed to the use of large thermal protection blankets on the orbiter’s upper body, rather than individual tiles requiring more attention.
879|
880|Weighing in at 151,315 pounds when it rolled out of the assembly plant in Palmdale, Calif., Atlantis was nearly 3.5 tons lighter than Columbia. The new orbiter arrived at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on April 9, 1985, and over the next seven months was prepared for her maiden voyage.
881|
882|Like her seafaring predecessor, orbiter Atlantis \carried on the spirit of exploration with several important missions of her own. On Oct. 3, 1985, Atlantis launched on her first space flight, STS 51-J, with a classified payload for the U.S. Department of Defense. The vehicle went on to carry four more DOD payloads on later missions.
883|
884|Atlantis also served as the on-orbit launch site for many noteworthy spacecraft, including planetary probes Magellan and Galileo, as well as the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory. An impressive array of onboard science experiments took place during most missions to further enhance space research in low Earth orbit.
885|
886|Starting with STS-71, Atlantis pioneered the Shuttle-Mir missions, flying the first seven missions to dock with the Russian space station. When linked, Atlantis and Mir together formed the largest spacecraft in orbit at the time. The missions to Mir included the first on-orbit U.S. crew exchanges, now a common occurrence on the International Space Station. On STS-79, the fourth docking mission, Atlantis ferried astronaut Shannon Lucid back to Earth after her record-setting 188 days in orbit aboard Mir.
887|
888|In recent years, Atlantis has delivered several vital components to the International Space Station, including the U.S. laboratory module, Destiny, as well as the Joint Airlock Quest and multiple sections of the Integrated Truss structure that makes up the station’s backbone.
889|
890|**Construction Milestones – OV-104**
891|
892|January 29, 1979: Contract Award  
893|March 30, 1980: Start structural assembly of crew module  
894|November 23, 1981: Start structural assembly of aft-fuselage  
895|June 13, 1983: Wings arrive at Palmdale from Grumman  
896|December 2, 1983: Start of Final Assembly  
897|April 10, 1984: Completed final assembly  
898|March 6, 1985: Rollout from Palmdale  
899|April 3, 1985: Overland transport from Palmdale to Edwards

On March 13, 1978, the Enterprise was ferried atop the SCA to NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center, where it was mated with the external tank and solid rocket boosters and subjected to a series of vertical ground vibration tests. These tested the mated configuration’s critical structural dynamic response modes, which were assessed against analytical math models used to design the various element interfaces.

These were completed in March 1979. On April 10, 1979, the Enterprise was ferried to the Kennedy Space Center and mated with the external tank and solid rocket boosters and transported via the mobile launcher platform to Launch Complex 39-A. At Launch Complex 39-A, the Enterprise served as a practice and launch complex fit-check verification tool representing the flight vehicles.

It was ferried back to NASA’s Dryden Flight Research Facility on Aug. 16, 1979, and then returned overland to Rockwell’s Palmdale final assembly facility on Oct. 30, 1979. Certain components were refurbished for use on flight vehicles being assembled at Palmdale. The Enterprise was then returned overland to the Dryden Flight Research Facility on Sept. 6, 1981.

From May of 1983 until Nov. 1985, Enterprise was ferried to the Paris, France, Air Show, as well as to Germany, Italy, England and Canada, to Vandenberg Air Force Base in California and to Mobile, Ala. From there it was taken by barge to New Orleans, La., for the United States 1984 World’s Fair. It was then ferried to Vandenberg Air Force Base and used as a practice and fit-check verification tool. Afterwards, the Enterprise was ferried from Vandenberg Air Force Base to NASA’s Dryden Flight Research Facility. Eventually, Enterprise was ferried from the Kennedy Space Center to Dulles Airport, Washington, D.C., and became the property of the Smithsonian Institution. The Enterprise was built as a test vehicle and is not equipped for space flight.

Following in the Enterprise’s creation, the orbiter Columbia was created and became the first Space Shuttle to fly into Earth orbit in 1981. Columbia was lost in its return flight in 2003. Four sister ships joined the fleet over the next 10 years: Challenger, arriving in 1982 but destroyed four years later; Discovery, 1983; Atlantis, 1985; and Endeavour, built as a replacement for Challenger, 1991.

**Construction Milestones**

July 26, 1972: Contract Award

June 4, 1974: Start structural assembly of Crew Module

August 26, 1974: Start structural assembly of aft-fuselage

May 23, 1975: Wings arrive at Palmdale from Grumman

August 24, 1975: Start of Final Assembly

March 12, 1975: Completed final assembly

September 17, 1976: Rollout from Palmdale

January 31, 1977: Overland transport from Palmdale to Edwards

April 10, 1979: Delivery to Kennedy Space Center

Enterprise, the first Space Shuttle Orbiter, was originally to be named Constitution (in honor of the U.S. Constitution's Bicentennial). However, viewers of the popular TV Science Fiction show Star Trek started a write-in campaign urging the White House to rename the vehicle to Enterprise.

Space Shuttle orbiters go by a more prosaic designation. Enterprise is commonly referred to as OV-101, for Orbiter Vehicle-101.

141|**Space Shuttle *Enterprise*** ([Orbiter Vehicle Designation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Vehicle_Designation "Orbiter Vehicle Designation"): **OV-101**) is the first [orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter") of the [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") system. Rolled out on September 17, 1976, it was built for [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") as part of the [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program") to perform atmospheric test flights after being launched from a [modified Boeing 747](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft").[[1]](#cite_note-tech-1) It was constructed without [engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_main_engine "Space Shuttle main engine") or a functional [heat shield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_shield "Heat shield"). As a result, it was not capable of [spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceflight "Spaceflight").[[2]](#cite_note-Slovinac2010-2)
142|
143|Originally, *Enterprise* had been intended to be refitted for [orbital flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_flight "Orbital flight") to become the second space-rated orbiter in service.[[1]](#cite_note-tech-1) However, during the construction of [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") [*Columbia*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia"), details of the final design changed, making it simpler and less costly to build  [*Challenger*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger") around a body frame that had been built as a [test article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_article_(aerospace) "Test article (aerospace)").[[1]](#cite_note-tech-1) Similarly, *Enterprise* was considered for refit to replace *Challenger* after the latter [was destroyed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster"), but  [*Endeavour*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour") was built from structural spares instead.[[1]](#cite_note-tech-1)[[3]](#cite_note-name-3)
144|
145|*Enterprise* was restored and placed on display in 2003 at the [Smithsonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s new [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") in Virginia.[[4]](#cite_note-4) Following the [retirement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_retirement "Space Shuttle retirement") of the Space Shuttle fleet,  [*Discovery*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery") replaced *Enterprise* at the Udvar-Hazy Center, and *Enterprise* was transferred to the [*Intrepid* Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intrepid_Museum "Intrepid Museum") in New York City, where it has been on display since July 2012.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

147|## Differences between *Enterprise* and future shuttles
148|
149|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Enterprise&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Differences between Enterprise and future shuttles")]
150|
151|The design of *Enterprise* was not the same as that planned for  [*Columbia*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia"), the first flight model; the aft fuselage was constructed differently, and it did not have the interfaces to mount [OMS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Orbital_Maneuvering_System "Space Shuttle Orbital Maneuvering System") pods. A large number of subsystems—ranging from main engines to radar equipment—were not installed on *Enterprise*, but the capacity to add them in the future was retained, as NASA originally intended to refit the orbiter for spaceflight at the conclusion of its testing. Instead of a [thermal protection system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system"), its surface was primarily covered with simulated tiles made from [polyurethane foam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyurethane_foam "Polyurethane foam"). [Fiberglass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiberglass "Fiberglass") was used for the leading edge panels in place of the [reinforced carbon–carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforced_carbon–carbon "Reinforced carbon–carbon") ones of spaceflight-worthy orbiters. Only a few sample thermal tiles and some [Nomex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomex "Nomex") blankets were real.[[6]](#cite_note-SI-Ent-6) *Enterprise* used [fuel cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuel_cell "Fuel cell") to generate its electrical power, but these were not sufficient to power the orbiter for spaceflight.[[7]](#cite_note-spaceline-7)
152|
153|*Platform to the Stars: Space Shuttle* (1980) Official NASA Space Shuttle program information film reel.
154|
155|*Enterprise* also lacked [reaction control system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reaction_control_system "Reaction control system") thrusters and hydraulic mechanisms for the landing gear; the landing gear doors were simply opened through the use of [explosive bolts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrotechnic_fastener "Pyrotechnic fastener") and the gear dropped down solely by gravity.[[7]](#cite_note-spaceline-7) As it was only used for atmospheric testing, *Enterprise* featured a large [nose probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitot_tube "Pitot tube") mounted on its nose cap, common on test aircraft because the location provides the most accurate readings for the test instruments, being mounted out in front of the disturbed airflow.
156|
157|*Enterprise* was equipped with [Lockheed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Corporation "Lockheed Corporation")-manufactured [zero-zero ejection seats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-zero_ejection_seat "Zero-zero ejection seat") like those its sister  [*Columbia*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") carried on its first four missions.[[7]](#cite_note-spaceline-7)

193|*Star Trek* creator [Gene Roddenberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Roddenberry "Gene Roddenberry") (third from right, in dark brown), the *Star Trek* cast (with the exception of [William Shatner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shatner "William Shatner")) and NASA administrators attending *Enterprise'*s rollout ceremony
194|
195|Construction began on *Enterprise* on June 4, 1974.[[1]](#cite_note-tech-1) Designated OV-101, it was originally planned to be named *Constitution* and unveiled on [Constitution Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_Day_(United_States) "Constitution Day (United States)"), September 17, 1976. Fans of [*Star Trek*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek:_The_Original_Series "Star Trek: The Original Series") asked [US President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") [Gerald Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ford "Gerald Ford"), through a letter-writing campaign, to name the orbiter after the television show's fictional starship, [USS *Enterprise*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Enterprise_(NCC-1701) "USS Enterprise (NCC-1701)").[[11]](#cite_note-:0-11)
196|
197|In an official memo, White House advisors cited "hundreds of thousands of letters" from [Trekkies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trekkie "Trekkie"), "one of the most dedicated constituencies in the country", as a reason for giving the shuttle the name.[[12]](#cite_note-popsci1-12) Although Ford did not publicly mention the campaign, the president said that he was "partial to the name" *Enterprise* because his naval unit had serviced the aircraft carrier [USS *Enterprise*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Enterprise_(CV-6) "USS Enterprise (CV-6)") (the ship for which *Star Trek'*s fictional craft was named) during World War II, and directed NASA officials to change the name.[[3]](#cite_note-name-3)[[13]](#cite_note-lewine19760906-13)[[14]](#cite_note-strauss20140710-14)[[11]](#cite_note-:0-11)
198|
199|In mid-1976 the orbiter was used for ground vibration tests, allowing engineers to compare data from an actual flight vehicle with theoretical models.[[1]](#cite_note-tech-1)
200|
201|On September 17, 1976, *Enterprise* was rolled out of [Rockwell's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockwell_International "Rockwell International") plant at [Palmdale, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmdale,_California "Palmdale, California"). In recognition of its fictional namesake, *Star Trek* creator [Gene Roddenberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Roddenberry "Gene Roddenberry") and most of the principal cast of the original series of *Star Trek* were on hand at the dedication ceremony.[[15]](#cite_note-Rioux2005-15)

203|### Approach and landing tests (ALT)
204|
205|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Enterprise&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Approach and landing tests (ALT)")]
206|
207|Main article: [Approach and Landing Tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests "Approach and Landing Tests")
208|
209|[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/HaiseandFullertonEnterprise.jpg/250px-HaiseandFullertonEnterprise.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HaiseandFullertonEnterprise.jpg)
210|
211|[Fred Haise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Haise "Fred Haise") and [Gordon Fullerton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Fullerton "Gordon Fullerton") (wearing oxygen mask) in *Enterprise*'s cockpit, 1977
212|
213|On January 31, 1977, *Enterprise* was taken by road to [Dryden Flight Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dryden_Flight_Research_Center "Dryden Flight Research Center") at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") to begin operational testing.[[1]](#cite_note-tech-1)[[16]](#cite_note-basics-16)
214|
215|While at NASA Dryden, *Enterprise* was used by NASA for a variety of ground and flight tests intended to validate aspects of the shuttle program.[[17]](#cite_note-alt-17) The initial nine-month testing period was referred to by the acronym *ALT*, for "Approach and Landing Test".[[1]](#cite_note-tech-1)[[18]](#cite_note-ff-18) These tests included a maiden "flight" on February 18, 1977, atop a [Boeing 747](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_747 "Boeing 747") [Shuttle Carrier Aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft") (SCA) to measure structural loads and ground handling and braking characteristics of the mated system. Ground tests of all orbiter subsystems were carried out to verify functionality prior to atmospheric flight.[[10]](#cite_note-nasasf20120427-10)
216|
217|The mated *Enterprise*/SCA combination was then subjected to five test flights with *Enterprise* uncrewed and unactivated. The purpose of these test flights was to measure the flight characteristics of the mated combination. These tests were followed with three test flights with *Enterprise* crewed to test the shuttle flight control systems.[[1]](#cite_note-tech-1)
218|
219|On August 12, 1977, *Enterprise* flew on its own for the first time.[[19]](#cite_note-Futz1977-19) *Enterprise* underwent four more free flights where the craft separated from the SCA and was landed under astronaut control. These tests verified the flight characteristics of the orbiter design and were used to carry out several aerodynamic and weight configurations.[[18]](#cite_note-ff-18) The first three flights were flown with a tailcone placed at the end of *Enterprise*'s aft fuselage, which reduced drag and turbulence when mated to the SCA. The final two flights saw the tailcone removed and mockup main engine nozzles installed. On the fifth and final glider flight, [pilot-induced oscillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot-induced_oscillation "Pilot-induced oscillation") problems were revealed, which had to be addressed before the first orbital launch occurred.[[17]](#cite_note-alt-17)
220|
221|[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Enterprise_lifted.jpg/250px-Enterprise_lifted.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Enterprise_lifted.jpg)

225|### Mated Vertical Ground Vibration Test (MGVT)
226|
227|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Enterprise&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mated Vertical Ground Vibration Test (MGVT)")]
228|
229|Following the conclusion of the ALT test flight program, on March 13, 1978, *Enterprise* was flown once again, but this time halfway across the country to NASA's [Marshall Space Flight Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Space_Flight_Center "Marshall Space Flight Center") (MSFC) in [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama") for the Mated Vertical Ground Vibration Testing (MGVT). The orbiter was lifted up on a sling very similar to the one used at Kennedy Space Center and placed inside the Dynamic Test Stand building, and mated to the Vertical Mate Ground Vibration Test tank (VMGVT-ET), which in turn was attached to a set of inert Solid Rocket Boosters (SRB) to form a complete shuttle launch stack, and marked the first time in the program's history that all Space Shuttle elements, an Orbiter, an External Tank (ET), and two SRBs, were mated together. During the course of the program, *Enterprise* and the rest of the launch stack would be exposed to a punishing series of vibration tests simulating as closely as possible those expected during various phases of launch, some tests with and others without the SRBs in place.[[20]](#cite_note-Baker2011-20)
230|
231|### Planned preparations for spaceflight
232|
233|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Enterprise&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Planned preparations for spaceflight")]
234|
235|At the conclusion of this testing, *Enterprise* was due to be taken back to Palmdale for retrofitting as a fully spaceflight capable vehicle. Under this arrangement, *Enterprise* would be launched on its maiden spaceflight in July 1981 to launch a communications satellite and retrieve the [Long Duration Exposure Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Duration_Exposure_Facility "Long Duration Exposure Facility"), then planned for a 1980 release on the first operational orbiter, *Columbia*. Afterward, *Enterprise* would conduct two [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") missions.[[21]](#cite_note-should-21) However, in the period between the rollout of *Enterprise* and the rollout of *Columbia*, a number of significant design changes had taken place, particularly with regard to the weight of the fuselage and wings. This meant that retrofitting the prototype would have been a much more expensive process than previously realized, involving the dismantling of the orbiter and the return of various structural sections to subcontractors across the country. As a consequence, NASA made the decision to convert an incomplete Structural Test Article, numbered STA-099, which had been built to undergo a variety of stress tests, into a fully flight-worthy orbiter, which became  [*Challenger*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger").

252|Following the MGVT program and with the decision to not use *Enterprise* for orbital missions, it was ferried to [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") on April 10, 1979. By June 1979, it was mated with an external tank and solid rocket boosters (known as a [boilerplate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boilerplate_(spaceflight) "Boilerplate (spaceflight)") configuration) and tested in a launch configuration at [KSC Launch Complex 39A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Launch_Complex_39 "Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39") for a series of fit checks of the facilities there.[[3]](#cite_note-name-3)
253|
254|After this period, *Enterprise* was returned to NASA's [Dryden Flight Research Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dryden_Flight_Research_Facility "Dryden Flight Research Facility") in September 1981.[[23]](#cite_note-ksc-pao-ent-23) In 1983 and 1984, *Enterprise* underwent an international tour visiting [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), and [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"). *Enterprise* also visited [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama"), and [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana") (while visiting the [1984 Louisiana World Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Louisiana_World_Exposition "1984 Louisiana World Exposition")).

258|*Enterprise* visited Vandenberg SLC-6 in launch configuration 17 months before [the first West Coast Shuttle launch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-62-A "STS-62-A") was scheduled
259|
260|Between November 1984 and May 1985, *Enterprise* was again mated with an external tank and solid rocket boosters in a boilerplate configuration for a series of fit checks of the [never-used shuttle facilities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Space_Launch_Complex_6 "Vandenberg Space Launch Complex 6") at [Vandenberg Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Air_Force_Base "Vandenberg Air Force Base") in California.[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-lompoc20050929-25)[[26]](#cite_note-telegramtribune19851016-26)
261|
262|On November 18, 1985, *Enterprise* was ferried to Washington, D.C., where it became property of the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution") and was stored in the [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum")'s hangar at [Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Dulles_International_Airport "Washington Dulles International Airport").

264|### Post-*Challenger*
265|
266|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Enterprise&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Post-Challenger")]
267|
268|After the [*Challenger* disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster"), NASA considered using *Enterprise* as a replacement. Refitting the shuttle with all of the necessary equipment for it to be used in space was considered, but NASA decided to use spare parts constructed at the same time as [*Discovery*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery") and [*Atlantis*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis") to build [*Endeavour*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour").[[3]](#cite_note-name-3)

278|In 2003 after the [breakup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") of  [*Columbia*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") during re-entry, the [*Columbia* Accident Investigation Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Accident_Investigation_Board "Columbia Accident Investigation Board") conducted tests at [Southwest Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Research_Institute "Southwest Research Institute"), which used an air cannon to shoot foam blocks of similar size, mass and speed to that which struck *Columbia* at a test structure which mechanically replicated the orbiter wing leading edge. They removed a section of fiberglass leading edge from *Enterprise*'s wing to perform analysis of the material and attached it to the test structure, then shot a foam block at it.[[27]](#cite_note-Harwood-27) While the leading edge was not broken as a result of the test, which took place on May 29, 2003, the impact was enough to permanently deform a seal and leave a thin gap 22 in (56 cm) long.[[28]](#cite_note-caib20030529-28)[[29]](#cite_note-usatoday20030529-29)[[30]](#cite_note-nytimes20030605-30) Since the strength of the [reinforced carbon–carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforced_carbon–carbon "Reinforced carbon–carbon") (RCC) on *Columbia* is "substantially weaker and less flexible" than the test section from *Enterprise*, this result suggested that the RCC would have been shattered.[[30]](#cite_note-nytimes20030605-30) A section of RCC leading edge from *Discovery* was tested on June 6, to determine the effects of the foam on a similarly aged leading edge, resulting in a three in (7.6 cm) crack on panel 6 and cracking on a T-shaped seal between panels 6 and 7.[[31]](#cite_note-caib20030606-31)[[32]](#cite_note-swri2003fall-32) On July 7, using a leading edge from *Atlantis* and focused on panel 8 with refined parameters stemming from the ... [truncated]
279|
280|The board determined that the probable cause of the accident was that the foam impact caused a breach of a reinforced carbon-carbon panel along the leading edge of *Columbia*'s left wing, allowing hot gases generated during re-entry to enter the wing and cause structural collapse. This caused *Columbia* to tumble out of control, breaking up with the loss of the entire crew.[[34]](#cite_note-nyt20030708-34)

308|From 1985 to 2003,[[10]](#cite_note-nasasf20120427-10) *Enterprise* was stored at the [Smithsonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s hangar at [Washington Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Dulles_International_Airport "Washington Dulles International Airport") before it was restored and moved to the Smithsonian's newly built [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum") [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") at Washington Dulles, where it was the centerpiece of the space collection.[[35]](#cite_note-hazy-35) On April 12, 2011, NASA announced that  [*Discovery*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery"), the most traveled orbiter in the fleet, would replace *Enterprise* in the Smithsonian's collection once the [Shuttle fleet was retired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_retirement "Space Shuttle retirement"), with ownership of *Enterprise* transferred to the [*Intrepid* Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intrepid_Museum "Intrepid Museum") in New York City. On April 17, 2012, *Discovery* was transported by [Shuttle Carrier Aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft") to Dulles from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), where it made several passes over the Washington D.C. metro area.[[36]](#cite_note-nasa20120417-36)[[37]](#cite_note-washpost20120418-37) After *Discovery* had been removed from the Shuttle Carrier Aircraft, both orbiters were displayed nose-to-nose outside the Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center before *Enterprise* was made ready for its flight to New York.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

326|On December 12, 2011, ownership of *Enterprise* was officially transferred to the *[Intrepid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intrepid_Sea,_Air_&_Space_Museum "Intrepid Sea, Air & Space Museum")* [Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intrepid_Sea,_Air_&_Space_Museum "Intrepid Sea, Air & Space Museum") in New York City.[[39]](#cite_note-cspace20111212-39)[[40]](#cite_note-NAS-40)[[41]](#cite_note-prweb20111122-41) In preparation for the anticipated relocation, engineers evaluated the vehicle in early 2010 and determined that it was safe to fly on the Shuttle Carrier Aircraft once again.[[42]](#cite_note-nsf100314-42) At approximately 13:40 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC "UTC") on April 27, 2012, *Enterprise* took off from Dulles International Airport en route to a fly-by over the [Hudson River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_River "Hudson River"), New York's [JFK International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JFK_International_Airport "JFK International Airport"), the [Statue of Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_Liberty "Statue of Liberty"), the [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_Bridge "George Washington Bridge") and [Verrazano–Narrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verrazano–Narrows_Bridge "Verrazano–Narrows Bridge") Bridges, and several other landmarks in the city, in an approximately 45-minute "final tour". At 15:23 UTC, *Enterprise* touched down at [JFK International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JFK_International_Airport "JFK International Airport").[[43]](#cite_note-njcom20120427-43)[[44]](#cite_note-wsj20120427-44)
327|
328|The mobile [Mate-Demate Device](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mate-Demate_Device "Mate-Demate Device") and cranes were transported from Dulles to the ramp at JFK and the shuttle was removed from the SCA overnight on May 12, 2012, placed on a specially designed flat bed trailer and returned to Hangar 12.[[45]](#cite_note-cspace20120301-45) On June 3 a [Weeks Marine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weeks_Marine "Weeks Marine") barge took *Enterprise* to [Jersey City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey_City "Jersey City"). The Shuttle sustained cosmetic damage to a wingtip when a gust of wind blew the barge towards a piling.[[46]](#cite_note-abcnews20120605-46) It was hoisted June 6 onto the Intrepid Museum in Manhattan.[[47]](#cite_note-njcom20120604-47)
329|
330|*Enterprise* went on public display on July 19, 2012, at the Intrepid Museum's new Space Shuttle Pavilion, a temporary shelter consisting of a pressurized, air-supported fabric bubble constructed on the aft end of the carrier's flight deck.[[48]](#cite_note-48)

332|[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Enterprise_nicked_tail_Sandy_jeh.jpg/250px-Enterprise_nicked_tail_Sandy_jeh.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Enterprise_nicked_tail_Sandy_jeh.jpg)

334|Damage from [Hurricane Sandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Sandy "Hurricane Sandy")
335|
336|On October 29, 2012, storm surges from [Hurricane Sandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Sandy "Hurricane Sandy") caused Pier 86, including the Intrepid Museum's visitor center, to flood, and knocked out the museum's electrical power and both backup generators. The loss of power caused the Space Shuttle Pavilion to deflate, and high winds from the hurricane caused the fabric of the Pavilion to tear and collapse around the orbiter. Minor damage was spotted on the [vertical stabilizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertical_stabilizer "Vertical stabilizer") of the orbiter, as a portion of the tail fin above the rudder/speedbrake had broken off.[[49]](#cite_note-space20121030-49) The broken section was recovered by museum staff. While the pavilion itself could not be replaced for some time in 2013, the museum erected scaffolding and sheeting around *Enterprise* to protect it from the environment.[[50]](#cite_note-space20121220-50)
337|
338|By April 2013, the damage sustained to *Enterprise*'s vertical stabilizer had been fully repaired, and construction work on the structure for a new pavilion was under way.[[51]](#cite_note-51) The pavilion and exhibit reopened on July 10, 2013.[[52]](#cite_note-52)
339|
340|*Enterprise* was listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") on March 13, 2013, reference number 13000071, in recognition of its role in the development of the Space Shuttle Program. The historic significance criteria are in space exploration, transportation, and engineering.[[53]](#cite_note-53)

165|**Space Shuttle *Discovery*** ([Orbiter Vehicle Designation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Vehicle_Designation "Orbiter Vehicle Designation"): **OV-103**) is a retired American [Space Shuttle orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter"). The [spaceplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceplane "Spaceplane") was one of the [orbiters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter") from [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program") and the third of five fully operational orbiters to be built.[[2]](#cite_note-ov103-2) Its first mission, [STS-41-D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D "STS-41-D"), flew from August 30 to September 5, 1984. Over 27 years of service it launched and landed 39 times, aggregating more spaceflights than any other spacecraft as of December 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit).[[3]](#cite_note-Guinness_most_spaceflights-3) The Space Shuttle launch vehicle had three main components: the [Space Shuttle orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter"), a single-use central fuel tank, and two reusable [solid rocket boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_rocket_booster "Solid rocket booster"). Nearly 25,000 [heat-resistant tiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") cover the orbiter to protect it from high temperatures on re-entry.[[4]](#cite_note-4)
166|
167|*Discovery* became the third operational orbiter to enter service, preceded by *[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")* and *[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")*.[[5]](#cite_note-5) After the *Challenger* and *Columbia* accidents, *Discovery* became the oldest surviving orbiter. It embarked on its final mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), on February 24, 2011, and touched down for the last time at [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") on March 9,[[6]](#cite_note-6) having spent a cumulative total of nearly a full year in space. *Discovery* performed both research and [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS) assembly missions, and also carried the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") into orbit among other satellites.
168|
169|*Discovery* was the first operational shuttle to be retired, followed by *[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")* and then *[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")*. The shuttle is now on display at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") of the [Smithsonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution") [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum").
170|
171|## History
172|
173|[[edit source](/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section's source code: History")]
174|
175|The name *Discovery* was chosen to carry on a tradition based on ships of exploration,[[2]](#cite_note-ov103-2) primarily [HMS *Discovery*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Discovery_(1774) "HMS Discovery (1774)"),[[7]](#cite_note-7) one of the ships commanded by Captain [James Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook "James Cook") during his third and final major voyage from 1776 to 1779, and [Henry Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hudson "Henry Hudson")'s [*Discovery*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(1602_ship) "Discovery (1602 ship)"),[[2]](#cite_note-ov103-2) which was used in 1610–1611 to explore [Hudson Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Bay "Hudson Bay") and search for a [Northwest Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Passage "Northwest Passage"). Other ships bearing the name have included [HMS *Discovery*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Discovery_(1874) "HMS Discovery (1874)")[[8]](#cite_note-8) of the 1875–1876 [British Arctic Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Arctic_Expedition "British Arctic Expedition") to the North Pole, and [RRS *Discovery*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RRS_Discovery "RRS Discovery"), which carried the 1901–1904 [*Discovery* Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Expedition "Discovery Expedition") to [Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica "Antarctica"), led by [Captain Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Falcon_Scott "Robert Falcon Scott").[[9]](#cite_note-pao-9)
176|
177|Space Shuttle *Discovery* launched the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") and conducted the [second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-82 "STS-82") and [third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-103 "STS-103") Hubble service missions. It also launched the [*Ulysses* probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_probe "Ulysses probe") and three [TDRS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_and_Data_Relay_Satellite_System "Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System") satellites. Twice *Discovery* was chosen as the "Return To Flight" Orbiter, first in 1988 after the [loss of *Challenger*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") in 1986, and then again for the twin "Return To Flight" missions in July 2005 and July 2006 after the [*Columbia* disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") in 2003. [Project Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury "Project Mercury") astronaut [John Glenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Glenn "John Glenn"), who was 77 at the time, flew with *Discovery* on [STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95") in 1998, making him the oldest person to go into space at that time in history.[[10]](#cite_note-over-10)
178|
179|Had plans to launch [United States Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") payloads from [Vandenberg Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Air_Force_Base "Vandenberg Air Force Base") gone ahead, *Discovery* would have become the dedicated [US Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Air_Force "US Air Force") shuttle.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Its first West Coast mission, [STS-62-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-62-A "STS-62-A"), was scheduled for 1986, but [canceled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canceled_Space_Shuttle_missions "Canceled Space Shuttle missions") in the aftermath of the *[Challenger disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_disaster "Challenger disaster")*.
180|
181|On May 27, 1999, *Discovery* was launched on [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96"), the first shuttle mission to dock with the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").[[12]](#cite_note-12)
182|
183|*Discovery* was retired after completing its final mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133") on March 9, 2011. The spacecraft is now on display in Virginia at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center"), an annex of the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum").[[13]](#cite_note-nasm-13)

243|During its construction, *Discovery* was fitted with several black tiles near the middle starboard window where there should have been white tiles. It is unknown if this was the result of a harmless manufacturing mishap or done intentionally to give a distinctive look to the shuttle. This feature has been called 'teardrop' and allowed *Discovery* to be told apart from the rest of the fleet without looking at its name, although often unnoticed by the uninitiated.[[14]](#cite_note-14)
244|
245|The spacecraft weighed roughly 6,870 lb (3,120 kg) less than *Columbia* when it was brought into service due to optimalizations determined during the construction and testing of *Enterprise*, *Columbia* and *Challenger*.[[10]](#cite_note-over-10) *Discovery* weighs 6 pounds (2.7 kg) heavier than *[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")* and 363 pounds (165 kg) heavier than *[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")* after further weight-saving adjustments were made.[[15]](#cite_note-FT_facts-15)
246|
247|Part of the *Discovery* weight optimizations included the greater use of quilted [AFRSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system#Flexible_Insulation_Blankets/Advanced_Flexible_Reusable_Insulation_(FIB/AFRSI) "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") blankets rather than the white [LRSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system#Low-temperature_reusable_surface_insulation_(LRSI) "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") tiles on the fuselage, and the use of [graphite epoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphite_epoxy "Graphite epoxy") instead of aluminum for the payload bay doors and some of the wing spars and beams.[[16]](#cite_note-16)
248|
249|Upon its delivery to the Kennedy Space Center in 1983, *Discovery* was modified alongside *Challenger* to accommodate the liquid-fueled [Centaur-G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centaur-G "Centaur-G") booster, which had been planned for use beginning in 1986 but was cancelled in the wake of the *Challenger* disaster.[[17]](#cite_note-17)
250|
251|Beginning in late 1995, the orbiter underwent a nine-month Orbiter Maintenance Down Period (OMDP) in [Palmdale, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmdale,_California "Palmdale, California"). This included outfitting the vehicle with a fifth set of cryogenic tanks and an external airlock to support missions to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"). As with all the orbiters, it could be attached to the top of specialized aircraft and did so in June 1996 when it returned to the Kennedy Space Center, and later in April 2012 when sent to the Udvar-Hazy Center, riding [piggy-back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piggy-back_(transportation) "Piggy-back (transportation)") on a [modified Boeing 747](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft").[[10]](#cite_note-over-10)
252|
253|After [STS-105](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-105 "STS-105"), *Discovery* became the first of the orbiter fleet to undergo Orbiter Major Modification (OMM) period at the Kennedy Space Center. Work began in September 2002 to prepare the vehicle for Return to Flight. The work included scheduled upgrades and additional safety modifications.[[10]](#cite_note-over-10)

267|*Discovery* was [decommissioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_decommissioning "Ship decommissioning") on March 9, 2011.[[19]](#cite_note-manifest-19)[[20]](#cite_note-CSCS1-20) NASA offered *Discovery* to the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum") for public display and preservation, after a month-long [decontamination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contamination_control "Contamination control") process,[[21]](#cite_note-21) as part of the national collection.[[22]](#cite_note-smithsonian-22)[[23]](#cite_note-smithsonian-houston-chronical-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24) *Discovery* replaced [*Enterprise*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise"), which was in the Smithsonian's display at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") until 2011.[[25]](#cite_note-25)[[26]](#cite_note-26)[[27]](#cite_note-27) *Discovery* was transported to [Washington Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Dulles_International_Airport "Washington Dulles International Airport") on April 17, 2012, and was transferred to the Udvar-Hazy Center on April 19 where a welcome ceremony was held. Afterwards, at around 5:30 pm, *Discovery* was rolled to its "final wheels stop" in the Udvar-Hazy Center.[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[29]](#cite_note-29)

269|Texas senators [John Cornyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cornyn "John Cornyn") and [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz "Ted Cruz") added a provision to the 2025 [One Big Beautiful Bill Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act "One Big Beautiful Bill Act") to spend $85 million to relocate a space vehicle that has flown astronauts into space, presumably *Discovery* because of the sponsors of the provision and previous legislation attempts, from the Udvar-Hazy Center to the [Space Center Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Center_Houston "Space Center Houston") Museum in Texas.[[30]](#cite_note-30)[[31]](#cite_note-31) While the Smithsonian estimated that the total cost of the transfer would be approximately $325 million, they also countered that ownership of the shuttle had been transferred to the museum and was no longer federal property, and that Congress did not have the ability to force a transfer.[[32]](#cite_note-32)[[33]](#cite_note-33)

277|## Flights
278|
279|[[edit source](/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section's source code: Flights")]
280|
281|By its last mission, *Discovery* had flown 149 million mi (240 million km) in 39 missions, completed 5,830 orbits, and spent 365 days in orbit over 27 years.[[34]](#cite_note-slt-34) *Discovery* flew [more flights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Orbiter#Flight_statistics "Space Shuttle Orbiter") than any other Orbiter Shuttle, including four in 1985 alone. *Discovery* flew both "return to flight" missions after the *[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_Disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger Disaster")* and *[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_Disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster")* disasters: [STS-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26 "STS-26") in 1988, [STS-114](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-114 "STS-114") in 2005, and [STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121") in 2006. *Discovery* flew the ante-penultimate mission of the Space Shuttle program, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), having launched on February 24, 2011. *Endeavour* flew [STS-134](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-134 "STS-134") and *Atlantis* performed [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135"), NASA's last Space Shuttle mission. On February 24, 2011, Space Shuttle *Discovery* launched from Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39-A to begin its final orbital flight.[[35]](#cite_note-ares6-35)

239|**Space Shuttle _Atlantis_** (Orbiter Vehicle designation: **OV‑104**) is a retired [Space Shuttle orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter") vehicle which belongs to [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA"), the [spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceflight "Spaceflight") and [space exploration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_exploration "Space exploration") agency of the United States.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-ov104-1)_Atlantis_ was manufactured by the [Rockwell International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockwell_International "Rockwell International") company in [Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_California "Southern California") and was delivered to the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") in Eastern [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida") in April 1985. _Atlantis_ is the fourth operational and the second-to-last Space Shuttle built.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-3) Its [maiden flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maiden_flight "Maiden flight") was [STS-51-J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-J "STS-51-J") made from October 3 to 7, 1985. It was, along with _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_, one of only two orbiters equipped to carry the [Shuttle-Centaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle-Centaur "Shuttle-Centaur") booster.
240|
241|_Atlantis_ embarked on its 33rd and final mission, and the final mission of the [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135"), on July 8, 2011. [STS-134](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-134 "STS-134") by [_Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour") was expected to be the final flight before STS-135 was authorized in October 2010. STS-135 took advantage of the processing for the STS-335 [Launch on Need](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_on_Need "Launch on Need") mission that would have been necessary if STS-134's crew became stranded in orbit.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-4)[_[new archival link needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Archiving\_a\_source "Help:Archiving a source")_]_Atlantis_ landed for the final time at the Kennedy Space Center on July 21, 2011.

286|Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ lifted off on its maiden voyage [STS-51-J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-51-J "STS-51-J") on October 3, 1985. This was the second shuttle mission that was a dedicated Department of Defense mission.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-8) It flew one other mission, [STS-61-B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-B "STS-61-B") (the second shuttle night launch) before the [_Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") temporarily grounded the shuttle fleet in 1986. Among the five Space Shuttles flown into space, _Atlantis_ conducted a subsequent mission in the shortest time after the previous mission (turnaround time) when it launched in November 1985 on STS-61-B, only 50 days after its previous mission, STS-51-J in October 1985. _Atlantis_ was then used for ten flights from 1988 to 1992. Two of these, both flown in 1989, deployed the planetary probes _[Magellan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magellan\_(spacecraft) "Magellan (spacecraft)")_ to [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus") (on [STS-30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-30 "STS-30")) and _[Galileo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo\_probe "Galileo probe")_ to [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter "Jupiter") (on [STS-34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-34 "STS-34")). With STS-30 _Atlantis_ became the first Space Shuttle to launch an interplanetary probe.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-9)

296|During the launch of [STS-27](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-27 "STS-27") in 1988, a piece of insulation shed from the right solid rocket booster struck the underside of the vehicle, severely damaging over 700 tiles and removing one tile altogether.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-10) The crew were instructed to use the remote manipulator system to survey the condition of the underside of the right wing, ultimately finding substantial tile damage. Due to the classified nature of the mission, the only images transferred to the [mission control center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_control_center "Mission control center") were encrypted and of extremely poor quality. Mission control personnel deemed the damage to be "lights and shadows" and instructed the crew to proceed with the mission as usual, infuriating many of the crew. Upon landing, Atlantis became the single-most-damaged shuttle to successfully land. The survival of the crew is attributed to a steel [L band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L_band "L band") antenna plate which was positioned directly under the missing tile.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-11) A similar situation would eventually lead to the [loss of the shuttle _Columbia_ in 2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"), albeit on the more critical reinforced carbon-carbon.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-12)
297|
298|During [STS-37](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-37 "STS-37") in 1991, _Atlantis_ deployed the [Compton Gamma Ray Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compton_Gamma_Ray_Observatory "Compton Gamma Ray Observatory"). Beginning in 1995 with [STS-71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-71 "STS-71"), _Atlantis_ made seven straight flights to the former [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia")[space station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station")_[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir")_ as part of the [Shuttle–_Mir_ program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle%E2%80%93Mir_program "Shuttle–Mir program"). STS-71 marked a number of firsts in human spaceflight: 100th U.S. crewed space flight; first U.S. Shuttle-Russian Space Station _Mir_ docking and joint on-orbit operations; and first on-orbit change-out of shuttle crew.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-13) When linked, _Atlantis_ and _Mir_ together formed the largest spacecraft in orbit at the time.

316|The longest mission flown using _Atlantis_ was [STS-117](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-117 "STS-117"), which lasted almost 14 days in June 2007.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-21) During STS-117, _Atlantis_' crew added a new starboard truss segment and solar array pair (the [S3/S4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure "Integrated Truss Structure") truss), folded the P6 array in preparation for its relocation and performed four spacewalks. _Atlantis_ was not equipped to take advantage of the [Station-to-Shuttle Power Transfer System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_system_of_the_International_Space_Station "Electrical system of the International Space Station") so missions could not be extended by making use of power provided by ISS.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-22)

318|During the [STS-129](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-129 "STS-129") post-flight interview on November 16, 2009, shuttle launch director Mike Leinbach said that _Atlantis_ officially beat [Space Shuttle _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery") for the record low amount of interim problem reports, with a total of just 54 listed since returning from STS-125. Leinbach added, "It is due to the team and the hardware processing. They just did a great job. The record will probably never be broken again in the history of the Space Shuttle Program, so congratulations to them."[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Leinbach made a similar report during a post-launch interview on May 14, 2010, saying that there were a total of 46 listed from STS-129 to STS-132.

320|## Orbiter maintenance down periods
321|
322|[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Atlantis&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Orbiter maintenance down periods")]
323|
324|_Atlantis_ went through two overhauls of scheduled [orbiter maintenance down periods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_maintenance_down_period?action=edit&redlink=1 "Orbiter maintenance down period (page does not exist)") (OMDPs) during its operational history.
325|
326|_Atlantis_ arrived at [Palmdale, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmdale,_California "Palmdale, California") in October 1992 for OMDP-1. During that visit 165 modifications were made over the next 20 months. These included the installation of a drag chute, new plumbing lines to configure the orbiter for extended duration, improved nose wheel steering, more than 800 new heat tiles and blankets, new insulation for main landing gear, and structural modifications to the airframe.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-23)
327|
328|On November 5, 1997, _Atlantis_ again arrived at Palmdale for OMDP-2 which was completed on September 24, 1998. The 130 modifications carried out during OMDP-2 included glass cockpit displays, replacement of TACAN navigation with GPS and ISS airlock and docking installation. Several weight reduction modifications were performed on the orbiter including replacement of Advanced Flexible Reusable Surface Insulation (AFRSI) insulation blankets[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-24) on upper surfaces with FRSI. Lightweight crew seats were installed and the [Extended Duration Orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_Duration_Orbiter "Extended Duration Orbiter") (EDO) package installed on OMDP-1 was removed to lighten _Atlantis_ to better serve its prime mission of servicing the ISS.
329|
330|During the standdown period post _Columbia_ accident, _Atlantis_ went through over 75 modifications to the orbiter ranging from very minor bolt change-outs to window change-outs and different fluid systems.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-25)
331|
332|_Atlantis_ was known among the shuttle workforce as being more prone than the others in the fleet to problems that needed to be addressed while readying the vehicle for launch, leading to some nicknaming it "[Britney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britney_Spears "Britney Spears")".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-26)

344|NASA initially planned to withdraw _Atlantis_ from service in 2008, as the orbiter would have been due to undergo its third scheduled OMDP; the timescale of the final retirement of the shuttle fleet was such that having the orbiter undergo this work was deemed uneconomical. It was planned that _Atlantis_ would be kept in near-flight condition to be used as a [spares source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannibalization_(parts) "Cannibalization (parts)") for _Discovery_ and _Endeavour_. However, with the significant planned flight schedule up to 2010, the decision was taken to extend the time between OMDPs, allowing _Atlantis_ to be retained for operations. _Atlantis_ was subsequently swapped for one flight of each _Discovery_ and _Endeavour_ in the flight manifest. _Atlantis_ had completed what was meant to be its last flight, [STS-132](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-132 "STS-132"), prior to the end of the shuttle program,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-27) but the extension of the Shuttle program into 2011 led to _Atlantis_ being selected for [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135"), the final Space Shuttle mission in July 2011.

352|The Visitor Complex displays _Atlantis_ with payload bay doors opened mounted at a 43.21° angle to give the appearance of being in orbit around the Earth.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-32) The mount angle pays tribute to the countdown that preceded every shuttle launch at KSC.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-33) A multi-story digital projection of Earth rotates behind the orbiter in a 5,900 m 2 (64,000 sq ft) indoor facility.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-35) Ground breaking of the facility occurred in 2012.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-36)

364|A total of 207 individuals flew with Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ over the course of its 33 missions.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-Atlantis_Legacy-38) Because the shuttle sometimes flew crew members arriving and departing Mir and the ISS, not all of them launched and landed on _Atlantis_.

366|Astronaut [Clayton Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson "Clayton Anderson"), ESA astronaut [Leopold Eyharts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopold_Eyharts "Leopold Eyharts") and Russian cosmonauts [Nikolai Budarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Budarin "Nikolai Budarin") and [Anatoly Solovyev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoly_Solovyev "Anatoly Solovyev") only launched on _Atlantis_. Similarly, astronauts [Daniel Tani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Tani "Daniel Tani") and [Sunita Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunita_Williams "Sunita Williams"), as well as cosmonauts [Vladimir Dezhurov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Dezhurov "Vladimir Dezhurov") and [Gennady Strekalov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gennady_Strekalov "Gennady Strekalov") only landed with _Atlantis_. Only 146 men and women both launched and landed aboard _Atlantis_.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-Atlantis_Legacy-38)
367|
368|Some of those people flew with _Atlantis_ more than once. Taking them into account, 203 total seats were filled over _Atlantis_' 33 missions. Astronaut [Jerry Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_L._Ross "Jerry L. Ross") holds the record for the most flights aboard _Atlantis_ at five.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-Atlantis_Legacy-38)
369|
370|Astronaut [Rodolfo Neri Vela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodolfo_Neri_Vela "Rodolfo Neri Vela") who flew aboard _Atlantis_ on STS-61-B mission in 1985 is the only Mexican to have traveled to space. ESA astronaut [Dirk Frimout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirk_D._Frimout "Dirk D. Frimout") who flew on STS-45 as a payload specialist was the first Belgian in space. STS-46 mission specialist [Claude Nicollier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Nicollier "Claude Nicollier") was the first astronaut from Switzerland. On the same flight, astronaut [Franco Malerba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco_Malerba "Franco Malerba") became the first citizen of Italy to travel to space.
371|
372|Astronaut [Mike Massimino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Massimino "Mike Massimino") who flew on STS-125 mission became the first person to use Twitter in space in May 2009.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-39)

424|NASA announced in 2007 that 24 helium and nitrogen gas tanks in _Atlantis_ were older than their designed lifetime. These [composite overwrapped pressure vessels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_overwrapped_pressure_vessel "Composite overwrapped pressure vessel") (COPV) were designed for a 10-year life and later cleared for an additional 10 years; they exceeded this life in 2005. NASA said it could not guarantee any longer that the vessels on _Atlantis_ would not burst or explode under full [pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressure "Pressure"). Failure of these tanks could have damaged parts of the orbiter and even wound or kill ground personnel. An in-flight failure of a pressure vessel could have even resulted in the loss of the orbiter and its crew. NASA analyses originally assumed that the vessels would [leak before they burst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressure_vessel#Leak_before_burst "Pressure vessel"), but new tests showed that they could in fact burst before leaking.

426|Because the original vendor was no longer in business, and a new manufacturer could not be qualified before 2010, when the shuttles were scheduled to be retired, NASA decided to continue operations with the existing tanks. Therefore, to reduce the risk of failure and the cumulative effects of load, the vessels were maintained at 80 percent of the operating pressure as late in the launch countdown as possible, and the launch pad was cleared of all but essential personnel when pressure was increased to 100 percent. The new launch procedure was employed during some of the remaining launches of _Atlantis_,[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-aging-52) but was resolved when the two COPVs deemed to have the highest risk of failure were replaced.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis#cite_note-copv-53)
